name: ip

examples.does: One line per interface: state and addresses
Routes, including the default gateway
Interfaces with state and MAC address
Which interface and gateway are used to reach an address
Packet, error and drop counters for one interface
Add an address until the next reboot (lasting changes go in netplan)

pitfalls: Changes made with ip are lost at reboot. On Ubuntu, lasting network settings live in /etc/netplan/.
ifconfig and route (net-tools) are old; ip replaces them.

name: ss
tasks: which process is using a port

examples.does: Listening TCP and UDP ports, with the process for each
Open TCP connections
Counts of sockets by type and state
Who listens on one port
TCP details per connection: round-trip time, window, retransmits

pitfalls: Without sudo, -p cannot show other users' processes.
netstat (net-tools) is old; ss replaces it.

name: ping

examples.does: Send 4 pings and show the results
Force IPv4
Test whether 1500-byte packets pass without fragmenting

pitfalls: No reply does not always mean down: firewalls often drop ping. Test the real port with nc -zv.

name: tracepath
summary: The route to a host, hop by hop

examples.does: Each hop on the way, as addresses, with the path MTU

name: mtr
summary: Live route and packet loss per hop

examples.does: A report after 10 rounds: loss and delay at each hop

pitfalls: Loss at one middle hop only is often just that router ignoring probes. Loss that continues to the end is real.

name: dig
tasks: which IP does a name resolve to

examples.does: Just the addresses for a name
Ask one particular DNS server
Reverse lookup: the name for an address
One record type (MX, TXT, NS, ...)

pitfalls: dig asks DNS directly. Programs also read /etc/hosts; getent hosts NAME shows what they really get.

name: resolvectl
summary: The DNS settings the server uses (systemd-resolved)

examples.does: DNS servers and search domains per interface
Resolve a name the way programs on this server do
Empty the DNS cache

pitfalls: /etc/resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.53, the local resolver. The real DNS servers are in resolvectl status.

name: curl
tasks: test a server before changing DNS

examples.does: Response headers only
Only the HTTP status code
Show the connection, TLS and headers step by step
Send the request to one server address, keeping the name (test before a DNS change)
Download a file under its own name, failing on HTTP errors

pitfalls: -k skips the certificate check. Use it only to diagnose, never in scripts.

examples.does: Download a file
Continue a download that was cut off
Save under a chosen name

name: netplan

examples.does: Apply the config; it rolls back after 120 seconds unless you confirm
Apply the config now, no rollback
Check the YAML and write the backend config, without applying it
The merged config from every file in /etc/netplan/

pitfalls: On a remote server, use netplan try, not apply: a mistake rolls back instead of cutting you off.
YAML uses spaces only. A tab or a wrong indent breaks the file.

name: ufw
tasks: allow a port from one network

examples.does: Firewall on or off, default policy and rules
Allow SSH

examples.cmd: sudo ufw allow from 192.0.2.0/24 to any port 5432 proto tcp
examples.does: Allow one port from one network only
Rules with numbers, for deleting
Remove a rule
Turn the firewall on (now and at boot)

pitfalls: On a remote server, allow SSH BEFORE ufw enable, or you lock yourself out.
Docker publishes ports past ufw rules; ufw does not protect published container ports.

examples.does: Every firewall rule, from ufw, iptables, Docker and others
Just the table names

name: iptables
summary: Firewall rules, older interface (uses nftables underneath)

examples.does: Rules with packet counts and numbers
Rules written as the commands that create them
Allow incoming SSH (until reboot unless saved)

pitfalls: Rules added with iptables are lost at reboot unless saved (e.g. the iptables-persistent package). On Ubuntu, ufw is the usual way.

name: tcpdump
tasks: save a capture to a file

examples.does: DNS packets on every interface, without name lookups
Traffic to and from one host on one port
Save 1000 packets to a file for Wireshark

pitfalls: Captures can hold passwords and private data. Delete the file when done.

name: ethtool
summary: Network card speed, driver and counters

examples.does: Speed, duplex and whether a link is detected
Driver and firmware version
The card's own counters, including errors

name: nc
tasks: can I reach the database port

examples.does: Can a TCP connection be opened to this port
Same, giving up after 3 seconds
Listen on a port, to test a firewall from the other side

pitfalls: Ubuntu's nc is the OpenBSD version; its options differ from other netcats.

name: ssh

examples.does: Log in
Log in on another port
Go through a jump host
Local port 8080 reaches port 80 on the server
Show each step of the login, to see why it fails

pitfalls: 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED' can mean a rebuilt server or an attack. Confirm the new key before removing the old one with ssh-keygen -R.

name: scp
tasks: copy a file to another server

examples.does: Copy a file to another server
Copy a folder, SSH on port 2222 (capital -P)

pitfalls: scp uses -P for the port; ssh uses -p.
For big or repeated copies use rsync: it can resume and skips unchanged files.

examples.does: Create a new key pair
Fingerprint of this server's host key (compare with what clients see)
Remove a server's old key from known_hosts

name: rsync
summary: Copy and sync files, locally or over SSH
tasks: copy a folder to another server

examples.does: Copy a folder, keeping permissions and times; only changed files
Show what a mirror would copy and delete, without doing it
Mirror: also delete files in the target that are gone from the source
Over SSH on port 2222, compressed, resumable, with progress

pitfalls: A slash at the end of the source matters: src/ copies what is inside src; src copies the folder itself.
Always run --delete with --dry-run first.
